article.para: Siliko Core includes a built-in infix parser that handles traditional mathematical expressions. Infix refers to the fact that, in this notation, the operator is placed between the operands on which it operates, as opposed to prefix notation, such as Lisp-style S-expressions, where the operator comes first, or suffix notation, such as reverse Polish notation, where the operator comes last. The Siliko infix language also includes support for function calls, using a syntax where the function name comes first, and its arguments are passed as a comma-separated list between parentheses after the function name. The Siliko infix language supports single mathematical expression without variables or state.

section.para: In all of these rules, operators are placed between the operands on which they function. Siliko’s infix language supports six operators: + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, / for division, ^ for exponentiation, and d for die rolls. Because addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division are left associative, the infix parser builds syntax trees in reverse when parsing sequences of these operators. These operators are also implemented as functions. The infix parser automatically generates function calls from these operations.
There are 13 productions that describe the Siliko infix language.
Every string of characters processed by the infix parser is called a line. A line consists of an expression, surrounded by whitespace, ending with a null character.
Whitespace consists of the tab, line feed, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return, and space characters. Except to separate tokens, whitespace is ignored by the lexical analyzer.

By layering the rules for expression, term, exponent, and roll into a heierarchy, the infix parser is able to properly implement the order of operations. An expression can be a simple term, without any plus or minus operators, or it can be a recursive expression followed by a plus or minus sign, followed by a term. If you recurse into the sub expresion enough, you should eventually run into a simple term, which will end the recursive chain and build the associativity for addition and subtraction operations. Because sub-expressions are evaluated before the expression they are a part of, thus ensuring that the leftmost operation is evaluated first.
A term is similar to an expression, but with exponent as the next layer and with the multiplication operator (as an asterisk, *) and division operator (as a forward slash, /) as the operators used.

A exponent differs from an expression or term by being right associative. This means that in a chain of exponents, the operation on the right is processed first. Because of this, the sub-exponent is on the right side in the formal grammar, but other than that the parsing looks the same. The components of an exponent are separated by a caret character (^). This character is used Because it resembles how the power is a small, superscript number following the base number.

The dice operator is neither right- nor left-associative; it only takes an atom as its first argument, and a non-negative integer as its second argument. Since the atom production is the end of the chain, there are no other rules to chain after a roll. The operator used for the dice operator is the lowercase letter d.

An atom is the final, unsplittable, rule at the base of Every expression. An atom can either be another expression between parentheses, a function call, or a number, Anything inside a pair of parentheses will be evaluated independently of any surrounding values and operations. A function call is handled independently of its surroundings naturally, and the only processing the prser does for numbers is to determine if they have a negative sign or not.
Function calls start with an ID, followed by an argument list between parentheses.

An identifier is any series of alphanumeric characters starting with a letter, except for d, e, pi, or a d immediately followed by a numeral. This exception for d followed by a numeral allows for notation like "3d6" to be used without needing to add a space between the dice roll operator and the number of faces.

An argument list is a comma-separated list of expressions. How many parameters a function takes is defined by the function, but Siliko Core’s parser requires at least one argument for any function call.
A number can be either an integer or a real, optionally proceeded by a minus sign (-).
An integer is a series of one or more decimal digits. The tokenizer passes the series of digits to the C standard-library strtoll function to get the integer value.

A real can take one of two forms. In the first form, it is is either the strings e, or pi. In the second form, it is a series of one or more decimal digits, followed by a decimal point, optionally followed by one or more decimal digits. The tokenizer passes the series of characters to the C standard-library strtod function to get the real value.
This grammar for the Siliko infix language uses the notation described in the Notation section of the W3 XML Recommendation.

production.rhs: expression space "+" space term | expression space "-" space term | term
term space "*" space exponent | term space "/" space exponent | exponent
